clue.text: They're a blow to Conservatism?

parts.note: winds deliver a literal blow, and forces for reform are the enemy of conservatism, so the phrase works both ways

explanation.surface: Something that deals a damaging blow to the Conservative Party or to traditional thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conservatism' tempts a political reading with a capital C, but the clue simply pairs wind that blows with the opposite of staying the same; the phrase was made famous by Harold Macmillan's 1960 speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Breezes that blow in reform are, by their nature, a threat to any instinct to keep things as they are.

clue.text: Wife formalised renewed expression of astonishment

indicators.note: something renewed is made over again, so the letters of formalised are built into a new form

explanation.surface: A husband's dismay at his wife making their arrangement official again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'renewed' looks like part of the story about the wife's paperwork, but it signals that the letters of formalised are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: People say this when they are too stunned or exasperated to find anything to say, an exclamation of amazement.

clue.text: Chemist's lack of alarm when speaking

indicators.note: the clue asks us to say the phrase out loud and write down a word that matches its sound

parts.note: having no bell means having nothing to ring as an alarm

explanation.surface: A pharmacist explains that their shop has no alarm system.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after Chemist stands for 'is', linking definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Nobel, the Swedish inventor of dynamite who founded the prizes, was trained as a chemist.

clue.text: Quick temper of female with uniform — wearing trousers, note

indicators.note: the trousers are worn around the other letters, so they go inside that garment

parts.note: shorts are short trousers
U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: A woman in uniform, wearing trousers, writes a note in a hot-headed mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wearing' puts FU inside SHORTS to give SHORTFUS, then E is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with a short fuse explodes quickly, an idiom for being easily angered.

clue.text: Charity event in Florida welcome in Australia

parts.note: Fla is the traditional abbreviation for the US state of Florida
g'day is the classic Australian greeting

explanation.surface: A fundraising event held in Florida, with an Aussie greeting.
explanation.walkthrough: A flag day is a British street collection where donors are given a small paper flag or sticker.
explanation.definitionFit: On such a day volunteers collect money for a cause in the street, handing out little flags as tokens.

clue.text: Trips with school society

parts.note: a high school is a kind of school, so high can stand for it

explanation.surface: Outings organised jointly by a school and a society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trips' looks like excursions; it means drug-induced experiences.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug trip and a high are both a spell of intoxicated euphoria, so the plurals are synonyms.

clue.text: Element in UN put me off

indicators.note: off here means gone wrong, so the letters of the phrase are spoiled into a new order

explanation.surface: Something in the United Nations has turned me off.
explanation.walkthrough: Element 93, named after the planet beyond Uranus.
explanation.definitionFit: This radioactive metal is chemical element number 93, a member of the actinide series.

clue.text: Girl's flat unfinished

indicators.note: the word is left without its final letter, so it is not finished

parts.note: a flat surface is an even one

explanation.surface: A young woman's apartment hasn't been completed yet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flat' looks like an apartment but means level; the 's after Girl is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eve is a common female first name, and crosswords often use any name as a girl or boy.

clue.text: Seafood, cold, local sent back

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

indicators.note: a dish sent back is returned, so the word is turned round

parts.note: a local is a British pub, the bar near home

explanation.surface: A seafood dish, served cold at the pub, is returned to the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'local' is British slang for one's neighbourhood pub, here its bar; 'sent back' turns that word round.
explanation.definitionFit: This ten-legged crustacean is a popular shellfish eaten as seafood.

clue.text: Zest of primate left clutching sword

indicators.note: the outer letters hold the sword in their grip, so it sits inside them

parts.note: orang is short for orangutan, a great ape
an epee is a fencing sword

explanation.surface: An ape on the left holds a sword with great energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zest' seems to mean enthusiasm; it is the outer skin of citrus fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Zest is the grated outer rind of citrus fruit used in cooking, the coloured skin of the fruit.

clue.text: Single idea lost in translation

indicators.note: translating changes the form of the words, so these letters are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: A single notion gets lost when rendered into another language.
explanation.definitionFit: Something isolated stands alone, one by itself, apart from others.

clue.text: Marrow jam

definitions.meaning: a marrow is a large vegetable of the gourd family
to jam is to cram or crush things tightly together

explanation.surface: A recipe for marrow jam, a British preserve.
explanation.walkthrough: A marrow is a large British squash vegetable; 'jam' is not the preserve but the verb to cram.
explanation.definitionFit: Marrows belong to the gourd family of vegetables; separately, to cram things together is to crush them into a tight space.

clue.text: Serial killer sugared rum to entrap marshal

indicators.note: the outer letters catch the marshal and hold him inside

parts.note: sugared food is sweet
Michel Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals
rum means strange or odd

explanation.surface: A murderer laces rum with sugar to snare a lawman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'marshal' looks like a US lawman; it is Napoleon's Marshal Ney.
explanation.definitionFit: The demon barber of Fleet Street in Victorian penny dreadfuls and later Sondheim's musical murders his customers one after another.

clue.text: S American rang up AA a year after crashing

indicators.note: a crash wrecks the shape of things, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A South American motorist phones the Automobile Association a year after an accident.
explanation.walkthrough: The AA is the British motoring breakdown service.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Paraguay, the landlocked country in South America, is a South American.

clue.text: Equivocal claim to generosity by posh old American

parts.note: someone claiming to be generous might say 'I am big', big meaning magnanimous
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U

explanation.surface: An elderly upper-class American boasts of being generous, but evasively.
explanation.walkthrough: U for posh comes from 'U and non-U', 1950s labels for upper-class and other British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A statement open to more than one interpretation is vague and unclear, which is what equivocal also means.

clue.text: Drug agent I figure out on reflection is a plant

parts.note: narc is American slang for a narcotics officer

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror is reversed, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to suss is to work out or figure out

explanation.surface: A narcotics officer works out, after some thought, that something is a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on reflection' turns SUSS into SSUS. 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: This genus of flowering bulbs includes daffodils and jonquils, so it names a plant.

clue.text: 13th or 15th, team's heading into last place

indicators.note: the first letter of the word goes to the end, the head moving to the back

parts.note: a side is a team; the 's means the team has its first letter moved

explanation.surface: On a calendar date, a team's leader drops to the bottom of the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading into last place' moves the S of SIDE to the end. In the Roman calendar the Ides fell on the 15th of March, May, July and October and the 13th of other months.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman calendar the Ides was the middle day of the month, the 13th or 15th depending on the month.

clue.text: In which one could be expecting stick

definitions.text: In which one could be expecting
definitions.meaning: British slang for pregnant, so this is where an expectant mother is
a heavy stick used as a weapon

explanation.walkthrough: 'In the club' is British slang for pregnant.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for pregnancy places one inside this word; separately a cudgel is a stout stick.

clue.text: Ace having people following India in test

indicators.note: the outer word has, that is holds, the other letters within it

parts.note: an ace is an expert

indicators.note: the people come after India in the string

parts.note: I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet
men means people

explanation.surface: A top player in the test, with people coming after the Indian side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having' puts IMEN, the people placed after India by 'following', inside EXPERT. 'test' suggests a cricket Test match.
explanation.definitionFit: A scientific trial carried out to check a hypothesis is a test of it.

clue.text: End of contract entered into by Post Office

indicators.note: the Post Office goes inside the other word, entering it

parts.note: to purse one's lips is to contract them

explanation.surface: The termination of a contract is handled by the Post Office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contract' looks like a legal agreement; it is the verb, as in pursing the lips.
explanation.definitionFit: End in the sense of an aim or goal, as in 'to what end', means the intention behind something.

clue.text: Display containing goods one can't choose?

indicators.note: the first word holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: to bear a mark or sign is to display it
G stands for good, so two goods give two Gs

explanation.surface: A shop display holding goods that a customer may not pick from.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the saying 'beggars can't be choosers', hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says those who ask for charity must accept whatever is offered, so they have no choice.

clue.text: Stick with popular French form master

parts.note: a rod is a stick
in means popular or fashionable

explanation.surface: A French schoolmaster in charge of a form uses the cane on popular pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form master' looks like a teacher in charge of a British school class; it is a master of sculpted form.
explanation.definitionFit: Auguste Rodin, maker of The Thinker, was a French sculptor, a master of three-dimensional shape.

clue.text: Tracks one in run continuously

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

indicators.note: the one is placed in the middle of the other letters, sitting inside them

parts.note: always means continuously
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Footprints show a single runner going on without a break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts I inside RALWAYS.
explanation.definitionFit: Railway lines are the tracks trains run on, so the plural names those systems of rails.

clue.text: I'll do that when I'm legally called on, initially

indicators.note: only the first letter of each of the words that follow is taken

explanation.surface: Someone promises to do a task when they are formally required to.
explanation.walkthrough: This radio procedure word is short for 'will comply'.
explanation.definitionFit: In radio procedure this word means 'will comply', a promise to carry out an instruction.

clue.text: No longer having to conduct tourist periodically alfresco

parts.note: if a shop is out of something it no longer has it
to do business is to conduct it

indicators.note: letters are taken at regular intervals, here the second, fourth and sixth

explanation.surface: No longer obliged to guide a tourist now and then in the open air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'periodically' takes the even letters of tourist, ORS.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfresco, borrowed from Italian, means in the open air, outside rather than inside a building.

clue.text: German city firm ludicrously upset hosts

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the letters read from bottom to top
the phrase plays host to the city, holding its letters within

explanation.surface: A German city's business is absurdly overturned while entertaining guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hosts' gives MLU from firm ludicrously, and 'upset' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulm is a city on the Danube in Baden-Württemberg, known as Einstein's birthplace.

clue.text: Reversed bank's repeated instructions

indicators.note: the word is turned round and read from the end back to the start

parts.note: to pool money is to bank it together; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A bank goes back on the standing orders it was given over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: In programming a loop is a block of instructions run again and again.
explanation.definitionFit: In computing, a block of code executed again and again until a condition is met is the classic repeated sequence.

clue.text: Read wrong notes: foreign articles tolerated

parts.note: mi is a note of the sol-fa scale, so mis are notes
un is French and der German for 'a' and 'the'
stood means tolerated, as in 'stood for it'

explanation.surface: Someone misreads notes, and foreign items were put up with.
explanation.definitionFit: To take the wrong meaning from something is to have interpreted or grasped it incorrectly.
